title: What Is a Youth Football Report? A Parent's Complete Guide
subtitle: What's inside a professional player report, what the scores actually mean, and how families use them to guide development.
content_md:
Every weekend, thousands of young players do something special on a pitch — and nobody writes it down. A **youth football report** changes that. It turns one match into a permanent, professional record of what your child can already do and what to train next.

This guide explains what a proper report contains, what the numbers really mean, and how families actually use them.

## What is a youth football report?

A youth football report is a structured, written evaluation of a single player based on real match footage. Instead of a coach's quick comment after training, it gives you:

- **Objective scores** across the core areas of the game
- **Evidence** — timestamps of the exact moments that earned each score
- **Context** — how the performance compares to realistic expectations for the player's age group
- **A development plan** — what to work on over the next 7, 30 and 90 days

The best reports are built from video, not memory. Video doesn't forget, doesn't play favourites, and lets an evaluator watch a decisive moment five times before writing a single word.

## What's actually inside a professional report?

At ScoutMePlay, every full report is built on four pillars — the same framework academies use when they assess trialists:

### 1. Technical
First touch, ball control, passing quality, striking technique, dribbling under pressure. Can the player execute the basics *when it matters*, not just in warm-ups?

### 2. Tactical
Positioning, decision speed, movement off the ball, awareness of space. This is the area parents most often underestimate — and the one scouts watch first.

### 3. Physical
Speed over the metres that decide duels, acceleration, balance, work rate. Measured against age-appropriate benchmarks, never against adults.

### 4. Mentality
Reaction after a mistake, bravery on the ball, communication, persistence. One recovered ball after a bad pass can say more than three completed dribbles.

Each pillar gets a score out of 10, and — crucially — a written explanation of *why*, backed by moments from the video with timestamps you can rewatch.

## What do the scores actually mean?

A 7.8 means nothing on its own. A good report translates every number into plain language a family can act on. For example:

> **Technical 8.4** — "His first touch buys him time other players his age don't have. See 14:32, where he controls a bouncing ball under pressure and plays forward in one motion."

That's the difference between a *statistic* and an *insight*. If a report only gives you numbers without evidence, it isn't telling you much.

## How do families use these reports?

- **To guide training.** Instead of "practise more", you get specific, prioritised work: e.g. weak-foot passing before new skill moves.
- **To track progress.** Two reports six months apart show development in black and white — incredibly motivating for young players.
- **To prepare for trials.** Knowing your strengths (and how to show them) changes how a player approaches an academy trial day.
- **To build confidence.** Seeing strengths written down by an independent professional is powerful for a young player's self-belief.

## What a report is NOT

An honest report will never promise a professional contract or guarantee an academy place. Anyone selling that promise should be avoided. What a report *can* do is make sure that when opportunity comes, your player knows exactly where they stand and what they've been building.

## How to get a report for your child

The process at [ScoutMePlay](/upload) is simple:

1. **Film one match** (a phone at the halfway line is enough — see our [filming guide](/blog/how-to-film-football-match-tips))
2. **Upload the clip and mark your player**
3. **Get the free preview**, then unlock the full report with scores, timestamped moments and a personal training plan

You can read more about how players are graded on our [methodology page](/methodology).

*One match. One report. A whole new way to see your child's game.*

title: How Football Scouts Actually Evaluate Young Players (U7–U21)
subtitle: The criteria real scouts use at every age group — and why the flashiest player on the pitch often isn't the one they write down.
content_md:
Ask ten parents what a scout looks for and most will say the same thing: goals. Ask a scout, and you'll get a very different answer.

Here's how experienced evaluators actually watch a youth match — and what they write down.

## The first thing a scout notices isn't the ball

Before a player ever receives a pass, scouts are watching:

- **Scanning** — does the player check their shoulders before the ball arrives?
- **Body shape** — are they positioned to play forward, or will they need an extra touch?
- **Movement** — do they drift into space, or wait for the game to come to them?

These habits predict how a player will cope at higher levels, where time on the ball shrinks every season. A player who scans twice before receiving is solving the game *before* it happens.

## What scouts look for by age group

### U7–U10: Love of the ball
At this age, evaluators want to see comfort in possession, bravery to try things, and joy. Nobody is measuring sprint speed. The question is simple: *does this child want the ball?*

### U11–U14: Decisions appear
Now the game gets its structure. Scouts start noting decision speed, first touch direction, 1v1 courage on both sides of the ball, and how a player reacts to mistakes. Physical differences are huge at this age — good scouts actively discount early growth spurts.

### U15–U18: The complete picture
Positioning, tactical discipline, consistency across a full match, physical duels, and mentality under pressure. This is where the four pillars — technical, tactical, physical, mentality — get weighed together seriously.

### U19–U21: Can it survive adult football?
The final question: do the player's strengths still function at senior intensity? A brilliant youth dribbler who can't protect the ball against grown defenders has a development gap, not a career-ending flaw — but it must be named and trained.

## The mistake-reaction test

Almost every experienced scout has a version of this: *ignore the mistake, watch the next five seconds.*

A misplaced pass tells you little. What the player does immediately afterwards tells you a lot:

- Sprints to win the ball back → **competitive character**
- Hides from the next pass → **confidence risk**
- Demands the ball again straight away → **the mentality academies want**

## Why video is changing youth scouting

A scout at a pitch sees a player for 60 minutes, once, often in bad weather with three other matches happening around them. Video changes the equation:

- Every touch can be rewatched and verified
- One player can be isolated and followed for the whole match
- Development can be compared across months, not memories

That's the principle behind [ScoutMePlay's reports](/upload): one match filmed on a phone becomes a permanent, evidence-based record — with every score tied to a timestamp a scout (or a parent) can check.

## What you can do with this as a parent

1. **Stop counting goals.** Start noticing scanning, movement and reactions.
2. **Film matches.** Not for social media — for evidence. Our [filming guide](/blog/how-to-film-football-match-tips) shows the simple setup.
3. **Get an independent read.** A structured [youth football report](/blog/youth-football-report-parents-guide) shows where your player genuinely stands, without a club's politics or a parent's heart in the way.

The flashiest player on the pitch gets the applause. The player who scans, moves and reacts gets written down.

title: How to Film a Football Match So Your Child's Talent Actually Shows
subtitle: The exact phone setup, position and settings that make match footage usable for real analysis — no fancy gear required.
content_md:
A single well-filmed match is worth more to your child's development than a season of highlight clips. It's evidence: what they did, when, and under how much pressure.

The good news: you don't need a camera drone or an editing suite. You need a phone, a position, and five rules.

## The setup (2 minutes, no gear shame)

- **Phone:** any modern smartphone. Landscape mode, always.
- **Tripod:** a €15 phone tripod transforms your footage. Shaky video hides talent.
- **Position:** halfway line, elevated if possible (a small hill, a stand, even standing on a bench). Height shows spacing and movement — the things evaluators actually study.
- **Distance:** far enough that roughly a third of the pitch is visible around the ball.

## The five rules of usable match footage

### 1. Follow the game, not your child
The most common mistake. Zoomed-in solo shots of your player destroy the context — nobody can judge a pass without seeing the options the player had. Keep a wide frame and pan smoothly with play.

### 2. Never stop recording
Record full halves, not moments. The best actions are unpredictable, and the "boring" minutes contain the off-ball movement that separates good players from noticed players.

### 3. Keep zoom to a minimum
Digital zoom eats quality fast. Stay wide; modern analysis can isolate a single marked player from a normal wide shot — that's exactly how [ScoutMePlay's tracking](/methodology) works.

### 4. Lock exposure before kickoff
Point at the pitch, hold to lock focus/exposure, then leave it alone. This prevents the mid-match "brightness pumping" that ruins otherwise great footage.

### 5. Storage and battery are part of the plan
A full match in 1080p needs roughly 8–10 GB and plenty of battery. Clear space the night before. 1080p at 30fps is the sweet spot — 4K adds file size, not analytical value.

## Where to stand (and where never to stand)

**Best:** halfway line, elevated, sun behind you.

**Acceptable:** halfway line at pitch level — get *any* height you can.

**Avoid:** behind the goal (distorts every distance), pitch corners (half the game is invisible), and moving along the sideline while recording (nauseating and unusable).

## What about matchday lighting and weather?

- **Low sun:** film with the sun behind the camera, even if it means the "wrong" side of the pitch.
- **Rain:** a sandwich bag with a hole for the lens is genuinely fine.
- **Evening/floodlights:** modern phones handle this well — just lock exposure (rule 4).

## After the match: what to do with the footage

1. **Don't edit.** Full, unedited halves are more valuable than any highlight reel — cuts remove the context that gives actions meaning.
2. **Upload as-is.** At [ScoutMePlay](/upload) you upload the raw clip, mark your player once, and the analysis follows that player through the whole match.
3. **Save the original.** Footage from six months ago becomes gold when you want to see progress in black and white.

## One match is enough to start

Parents often wait for "a good match" to film. Don't. The most useful report often comes from an ordinary performance — that's the baseline all future development gets measured against.

Film the next match. Whatever it turns out to be, it's the start of the record — and you can turn it into a full [youth football report](/blog/youth-football-report-parents-guide) the same day.

title: The 4 Pillars of Player Development: Technical, Tactical, Physical, Mentality
subtitle: The framework academies use to develop complete players — and how to train each pillar at home without burning your child out.
content_md:
Every serious football academy on earth evaluates players through some version of the same four lenses. Different logos, same framework: **Technical. Tactical. Physical. Mentality.**

Understanding these four pillars changes how you watch your child play — and how you help them improve without adding pressure.

## Pillar 1: Technical — can you execute?

Technical skill is the ability to carry out football actions cleanly under match conditions: first touch, passing over different distances, striking the ball, dribbling, shielding.

**What great looks like:** not tricks — *repeatability under pressure*. A player who completes a simple pass correctly 95 times out of 100 is technically stronger than one who lands a spectacular skill move once per match.

**Train it:** wall passes (both feet, 10 minutes daily beats an hour weekly), juggling with purpose (thigh–foot–head patterns), first-touch games where the touch must go *into space*, never dead under the body.

## Pillar 2: Tactical — do you understand the game?

Tactical ability is knowing where to be, when to move and what the best option is *before* the ball arrives. It's the least visible pillar from the sideline — and the first one scouts check.

**What great looks like:** scanning before receiving, movement that creates passing lanes, sensible decisions at speed, defensive positioning that closes danger before it exists.

**Train it:** watch matches *with* your child and ask "where should the ball go next?" before each pass; play small-sided games (3v3, 4v4) where every player touches the ball constantly; after their own matches, ask about decisions ("what did you see?"), never just results.

## Pillar 3: Physical — can your body deliver?

Speed, acceleration, agility, balance, endurance — always judged **against the player's own age group**, never against adults or early-developing teammates.

**What great looks like at youth level:** winning the first three metres, staying on the ball through contact, and repeating sprints in the final ten minutes as sharply as the first ten.

**Train it (age-appropriately):** short sprint games under 10 seconds, single-leg balance work disguised as play, and above all — enough sleep. No supplement outperforms sleep for a developing athlete. Avoid heavy strength work before the growth spurt; bodyweight is plenty.

## Pillar 4: Mentality — what happens after the mistake?

The pillar that decides careers. Bravery to demand the ball, resilience after errors, focus for a full match, coachability.

**What great looks like:** a player who misplaces a pass and *immediately* shows for the next one. A player who presses just as hard at 0–3 as at 0–0.

**Train it:** praise decisions and reactions, not just goals ("I loved how fast you won that ball back"); normalise mistakes as information; let them fail without a sideline commentary. Confidence grows in environments where trying things is safe.

## The pillars work together — and that's the point

A brilliant technician with weak mentality disappears in big matches. A tactical brain in an unfit body arrives at every idea too late. Development means knowing **which pillar is the current bottleneck** — and that's almost impossible to see from the sideline with a parent's eyes.

That's exactly what a structured evaluation is for. A [ScoutMePlay report](/upload) scores all four pillars from one match video, shows the timestamped evidence behind every score, and turns the weakest pillar into a concrete 7/30/90-day plan.

Watch your child's next match through these four lenses. You'll see a different game — and probably a different player — than you saw last weekend.

title: From Grassroots to Academy: A Realistic Roadmap for Ambitious Young Players
subtitle: How players actually get seen, what trial days really measure, and the honest timeline nobody tells families about.
content_md:
Let's start with honesty, because your family deserves it: most young players will not sign professional contracts — and a football journey can still be one of the most valuable things in a young person's life. Discipline, resilience, friendships, fitness, joy.

With that said: players *do* move from grassroots pitches to academies every single season. Here's how it actually happens.

## How players really get noticed

Forget the myth of the scout who magically appears at a random U10 match. In reality, visibility comes from a handful of channels:

1. **Coach recommendations** — grassroots coaches talk to academy coaches. Being coachable matters more than parents think.
2. **Local talent days and open trials** — published by clubs, open to everyone brave enough to show up.
3. **Playing up or against strong opposition** — tournaments against academy-affiliated teams are effectively live auditions.
4. **Video evidence** — increasingly the first filter. A clear match video and a structured [player report](/blog/youth-football-report-parents-guide) let a busy academy see in 10 minutes what would otherwise take three scouting trips.

Notice what's *not* on the list: expensive agents for 11-year-olds, paid "guaranteed exposure" schemes, and social-media trick videos. Evaluators care about match behaviour, not choreography.

## What a trial day actually measures

Parents imagine trials as skill contests. They're closer to *behaviour observations*:

- **First 15 minutes:** scanning, first touch, communication — the habits that survive nerves
- **Small-sided games:** decision speed and bravery in tight spaces
- **When things go wrong:** the recovery reaction (evaluators watch this deliberately)
- **Between drills:** listening, adjusting, encouraging teammates — coachability in the wild

A player who arrives knowing their own game — strengths named, weaknesses being worked on — behaves differently on trial day. Preparation shows.

## The realistic timeline

- **U7–U10:** development centres and fun. Academies cast wide, loose nets. No family should relocate a life at this stage.
- **U11–U14:** the first serious intakes. Also the age of the biggest selection mistakes (early developers look brilliant; late developers get missed — evaluators know this and increasingly correct for it).
- **U15–U16:** the funnel narrows sharply. Full-time academy places become genuinely competitive.
- **U17–U21:** late paths are real: lower-league clubs, strong amateur setups, university football, and semi-pro routes produce professionals every year. *Released at 16 is not the end of the story.*

## What families can control

You can't control who's watching. You can control:

1. **The training habit** — 20 focused minutes daily beats occasional marathons. Target the weakest of the [four pillars](/blog/four-pillars-player-development).
2. **The evidence** — film matches properly ([here's how](/blog/how-to-film-football-match-tips)) and build a record of development over time.
3. **The self-knowledge** — an independent evaluation, like a [ScoutMePlay report](/upload), tells a player exactly where they stand against age benchmarks, with video proof. That clarity is calming; guesswork is what creates pressure.
4. **The environment** — a child who still loves the game at 16 has beaten the biggest dropout cause in youth football.

## The message worth repeating

Getting seen is not luck anymore. Between open trials, tournaments and video, an ambitious player has more legitimate windows than any previous generation.

Keep the record. Do the work. Love the game. When the window opens, be ready — with evidence.

title: How to Help Your Child Bounce Back After a Tough Match
subtitle: A hard game can hurt, but it can also become one of the best learning moments in your child’s journey.
content_md:
Every young player has one.

A match where nothing comes off. A mistake leads to a goal. A heavy loss. A game where your child comes off quiet, angry or close to tears.

If you're wondering how to help your **child bounce back after a tough match**, you're not alone. In youth football, difficult afternoons are part of the journey. What matters most is what happens next: at home, in the car, at training and in the way your child talks to themselves.

The good news? Parents can make a big difference here.

Not by pretending the match was brilliant when it clearly wasn't.

Not by giving a long lecture either.

But by helping their child process the game honestly, calmly and constructively.

## Why tough matches matter more than we think

A bad result or poor performance can feel huge to a young player.

For children, football is rarely just football. It's identity, friendship, confidence, belonging and pride all wrapped into one. So when a match goes badly, the emotions can spill over fast.

Some players talk non-stop after the final whistle.

Others go silent.

Some blame themselves.

Some blame teammates, the referee or the coach.

All of those reactions are normal.

A tough match can actually reveal a lot about where your child is in their development, especially in the mental side of the game. If you've read our piece on [the 4 pillars of player development](/blog/four-pillars-player-development), you'll know mentality matters just as much as technical and physical growth.

The goal is not to remove disappointment.

The goal is to help your child handle it well.

## What to do in the first hour after the match

The first hour matters because emotions are still hot.

This is not usually the best time for a full post-match review.

### Start with comfort, not coaching

Keep it simple.

Try:
- "Tough one today."
- "I know that hurts."
- "I'm proud of you for seeing it through."
- "Let's get home and reset."

That kind of response tells your child they are safe with you, even when things go badly.

### Avoid the instant analysis

Try not to jump straight into:
- what they did wrong
- what the coach should have done
- what scouts might think
- whether they should have passed, pressed or tracked back

Even if your points are fair, they often won't land well in the emotional moment.

### Let them lead the first conversation

If they want to talk, listen.

If they don't, leave a little space.

A simple "Do you want to chat now or later?" works well.

That question gives them some control, which matters after a game where they may feel they've lost it.

## How to talk about a poor performance without knocking confidence

This is where many parents worry.

You want to be honest.

You also want to protect confidence.

You can do both.

### Focus on facts before feelings spiral

Bring the conversation back to specifics.

Instead of:
- "You were all over the place today."

Try:
- "You looked frustrated after the first mistake."
- "Their midfield pressed really well."
- "You kept showing for the ball even when it was tough."

Specific, grounded observations help children see the game more clearly.

### Separate the player from the performance

One bad match does not mean:
- they are not talented
- they are going backwards
- they are letting everyone down

Say it plainly:
- "You had a difficult game. That doesn't define you."
- "A poor match is an event, not your identity."

Young players need to hear that.

### Praise honest qualities

After a tough match, empty praise can feel false.

Real praise works better:
- effort
- bravery
- work rate
- attitude after mistakes
- willingness to keep trying

For example:
- "I liked that you kept asking for the ball."
- "You didn't hide."
- "You worked back even when the game was against you."

That's the kind of confidence that lasts.

## How to help your child bounce back after a tough match this week

The best response is practical.

Not dramatic.

Not a complete overhaul.

Just one or two useful next steps.

## How to help your child bounce back after a tough match with a simple reset plan

A reset plan keeps the week manageable.

Use this three-step approach.

### 1. Pick one learning point

Only one.

Not five.

Ask:
- "What's one thing you want to do better next game?"
- "What felt hardest today?"
- "What would you change if the same situation happened again?"

Examples:
- check shoulder earlier
- release the ball quicker
- recover mentally after a mistake
- be stronger in 1v1s
- communicate more

### 2. Turn it into one action at training

Link the lesson to something concrete.

For example:
- If they lost possession under pressure, work on first touch and scanning.
- If they faded after a mistake, practise a reset routine: deep breath, clap hands, next action.
- If they struggled physically, focus on movement and intensity in training.

Keep it small enough to act on this week.

### 3. End the week by noticing progress

Before the next match, ask:
- "What have you worked on since last weekend?"
- "What's one thing you'll try tomorrow?"

After the next match, look for improvement in that area.

Not perfection.

Progress.

## When your child is being really hard on themselves

Some young players feel every mistake deeply.

They replay moments all evening.

They compare themselves to teammates.

They worry they've ruined their chances.

This is where your tone matters most.

Remind them:
- every good player has difficult games
- development is rarely a straight line
- coaches and scouts do not judge a player on one moment alone

In fact, understanding the bigger picture can help. Our article on [how football scouts actually evaluate young players](/blog/how-football-scouts-evaluate-young-players) explains why decision-making, attitude and consistency matter so much over time.

If your child watches their match footage, do it carefully. Don't use video as a tool for blame. Use it to spot patterns and learning points. If you ever want a clearer, calmer breakdown, you can [upload a match video](/upload) and get a structured report built around real actions, not touchline emotion.

## What not to say after a bad game

Parents mean well.

But some phrases make recovery harder.

Try to avoid:
- "That was embarrassing."
- "You need to toughen up."
- "Scouts won't like that."
- "Your teammate was much better than you today."
- "If you want it enough, you'd have played better."

These comments can stick for a long time.

They may create fear rather than growth.

Instead, aim for honesty with warmth:
- "Yes, it was a difficult day. Let's learn from it."
- "What do you think happened?"
- "What's the next step?"

## If the problem keeps happening

Sometimes a tough match is just a tough match.

Sometimes it reveals a repeated issue:
- confidence drops after mistakes
- poor body language
- panic under pressure
- lack of positional understanding
- frustration affecting effort

If that happens, step back and look for trends rather than overreacting to one game.

This is where a more objective view helps. Reading about [what a youth football report is](/blog/youth-football-report-parents-guide) can give you a better sense of how structured feedback supports development. If you're curious about how those insights are built, you can also look at [our methodology](/methodology).

A calm, clear report can help families move away from guesswork and towards useful action.

## Your child needs your steadiness most on the hard days

It is easy to be the supportive parent when your child scores, wins and smiles all the way home.

The real test is the muddy drive back after a hard afternoon.

That is when your child notices your face, your voice and your patience.

They are learning from you how to deal with setbacks.

So if you're trying to help your **child bounce back after a tough match**, remember this:

You do not need the perfect speech.

You do not need to solve everything that day.

You just need to help them feel safe, seen and capable of improving.

One tough match does not write their story.

Handled well, it can strengthen it.

If you'd like a calmer way to review a game and spot real next steps, we're here when you need us. A clear look at the match can help turn disappointment into a plan, one step at a time.
